rewritten_text:
“I'm going, Master Will—I really am,” the black man answered promptly. “Almost at the end now.”

“At the end!” Legrand practically screamed. “Are you saying you're out at the end of that branch?”

“Nearly there, master—ohhhhh! Lord have mercy! What's this thing up in the tree?”

“Well!” cried Legrand, delighted. “What is it?”

“Why, it's just a skull. Someone's left his head up here, and the crows have eaten every scrap of flesh off it.”

“A skull, you say! Very good. How is it attached to the branch? What's keeping it there?”

“That's a good question, master. I'll have to look. Well, this is a very strange thing, I must say. There's a huge nail in the skull, fastening it to the tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do exactly what I tell you. Do you understand?”

“Yes, master.”

“Then listen carefully. Find the skull's left eye.”

“Ha! That's a good one! There aren't any eyes left in it.”

“Damn your stupidity! Can you tell your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that. I know all about it. My left hand is the one I chop wood with.”

“Of course! You're left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now I suppose you can find the skull's left eye, or the place where it used to be. Have you found it?”

There was a long silence. At last the black man asked:

“Is the skull's left eye on the same side as its left hand too? Because this skull doesn't have any hand at all. Never mind! I've found the left eye now—here it is! What should I do with it?”

“Lower the beetle through it until you reach the end of the string. But make sure you keep hold of the string.”

“Done, Master Will. It's easy enough to put the bug through the hole. Watch out for it down there!”

Throughout this conversation, Jupiter had remained entirely hidden from view. But the beetle he had lowered was now visible at the end of the string, shining like a ball of polished gold in the last rays of sunset, which still faintly lit the hill where we stood. The scarab hung well clear of every branch; if released, it would have dropped at our feet. Legrand immediately picked up the scythe and cleared a circle three or four yards across directly beneath the insect. Once he had finished, he told Jupiter to release the string and climb down from the tree.

In the middle of this opening I discerned a white speck, though at first I could not determine its nature. After adjusting the telescope's focus, I looked once more and recognized a human skull.

“On making this discovery, I felt so confident that I regarded the riddle as answered; for ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could signify nothing but the skull's situation in the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death's head’ likewise allowed only one construction in a search for concealed treasure. I understood that a bullet was to be dropped through the skull's left eye. A bee-line—that is, a straight line—taken from the nearest part of the trunk through ‘the shot,’ or the place at which the bullet landed, and continued fifty feet beyond it, would fix a particular spot. Beneath that spot, I thought, something valuable might very possibly have been buried.”

“This,” I observed, “is perfectly plain; ingenious though it is, it remains simple and definite. What happened after you departed from the Bishop's Hotel?”

“Having carefully determined the tree's bearings, I set out towards home. But the moment I stepped away from ‘the devil's seat,’ the round opening disappeared, and however I turned, I could not catch another glimpse of it. To my mind, the greatest ingenuity of the entire affair lies in the fact—and repeated trials have satisfied me that it is a fact—that this circular gap cannot be seen from any accessible position except the narrow shelf on the rock's face.

“Jupiter accompanied me on this visit to the ‘Bishop's Hotel.’ He had doubtless noticed my distracted manner during the preceding weeks, and was particularly careful never to leave me by myself. The following day, however, I rose exceedingly early, managed to elude him, and made my way into the hills to look for the tree. Much labour brought me to it at last. When I returned that evening, my valet offered to flog me. As to the remainder of our adventure, I believe your knowledge equals mine.”

“I presume,” said I, “that our first attempt at excavation missed the place because Jupiter foolishly lowered the beetle through the skull's right eye rather than its left.”

“Exactly. His error shifted the ‘shot’ by some two and a half inches—that is, it altered the position of the stake closest to the tree. Had the treasure lain directly under the ‘shot,’ the mistake would have mattered little. But the ‘shot’ and the nearest part of the tree were simply two points by which to determine a line's direction. Naturally, the deviation, however slight at its origin, grew as we followed that line; by the time we had covered fifty feet, it had led us entirely astray.

I turn now to my own story. There is little to tell about my early life, and I will keep it brief. Still, I must spend some time on my childhood. Only then can it be clear why the loss of one hope would leave my whole life empty, and why the destruction of the only love I was allowed to hold would destroy my life with it.

I have said that my aunt was very different from my father. I believe she had no trace of malice in her heart, yet it was the coldest heart any person ever possessed. She was incapable of affection. She took me into her care because she thought it was her duty. But she had lived too long alone, free from children's chatter and noise, to let me disturb her peace. She had never married. For the previous five years, she had lived entirely alone on an estate inherited from her mother, beside Loch Lomond in Scotland. In his letters, my father had asked her to live with me at his family home, in beautiful countryside near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused. Once she had settled the business left in her hands by her brother's departure, she left England and took me to her Scottish estate.

As a baby, and until I reached the age of eight, I was cared for by a servant of my mother's who had come with us to our secluded home for that purpose. I lived in a distant part of the house and saw my aunt only at fixed times. We met twice each day. Around noon she visited my nursery; after her dinner I was brought to her. She never embraced me. Throughout my time in her room, she seemed afraid that some childish impulse would make me troublesome. My good nurse carefully coached me before daring to take me into the parlour. My aunt's cold expression and few stiff words frightened me so much that I rarely forgot these lessons or broke the perfect stillness I was taught to maintain during our brief visits.

Under my kind nurse's care, I roamed freely through our park and the nearby fields. Born of a profound love, I showed a deeply sensitive nature from my earliest years. I cannot describe how passionately I loved everything around me, even objects that had no life.
